front: The ISTQB term for a human mistake (e.g. misreading the spec)
back: Error. It can lead to a defect in a work product, which can cause a failure when executed.

front: Where does the root cause sit in the error → defect → failure chain?
back: Before it: the root cause is why the error was made (e.g. time pressure, an ambiguous GDD). It is never a link in the chain.

front: The development approach the whole team approach comes from
back: Extreme Programming (XP). Not just "Agile".

front: The cognitive bias that makes it hard for authors to accept defects in their own work
back: Confirmation bias: a main reason for independent testing.

front: Traceability lets you find which tests to re-check after a requirement changes. The term for this?
back: Impact analysis.

front: Writing test cases vs organising them into suites and preparing test data: which two activities?
back: Test design (create the test cases), then test implementation (organise, prepare, get ready to run).

front: Testware produced by test execution vs by test completion
back: Execution: test logs, defect reports. Completion: test completion report, lessons learned (and archived testware).

front: Testing is a form of ___; quality assurance focuses on ___
back: Testing is quality control (product-oriented, corrective). QA is process-oriented and preventive.

front: QA team tests the whole game against the spec, then players and the publisher judge release readiness. Which two test levels?
back: System testing, then acceptance testing.

front: Functional vs non-functional testing in one line each
back: Functional: WHAT the system does. Non-functional: HOW WELL it does it (performance, usability, security…).

front: A field accepts 1–50. How many equivalence partitions, and which?
back: Three: below 1 (invalid), 1–50 (valid), above 50 (invalid). Valid = the spec says it is processed; invalid = rejected or not defined.

front: Listing likely defects from experience and designing tests to expose each one, methodically
back: Error guessing, in its methodical form: fault attacks.

front: The defining trait of exploratory testing
back: Tests are designed, executed and evaluated at the same time, while the tester learns about the test object.

front: Severity vs priority
back: Severity = the impact of the defect when it occurs (never how often). Priority = how urgently it should be fixed (a business call).

front: What counts as a static testing tool?
back: A tool that supports reviews and static analysis (linters, code analysers, review features). Wikis and chat are collaboration tools.

front: In an inspection, which two roles may the author never take?
back: Review leader and scribe. The author does take part.

front: The seven test activities, in order
back: PMADIEC: Planning, Monitoring and control, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Execution, Completion.

front: The seven testing principles, grouped
back: 2-3-2. Limits: testing shows presence not absence; exhaustive testing is impossible. Strategy: early testing saves time and money; defects cluster; tests wear out. Wisdom: testing is context dependent; absence-of-defects fallacy.

front: What does good traceability let you do? (five things)
back: CIRAP: Coverage evaluation, Impact analysis, Risk tracking, Audits, Progress reporting.

front: The four review types, from least to most formal
back: I-WTI: Informal review, Walkthrough, Technical review, Inspection.

front: The three parts of a user story
back: The 3 C's: Card, Conversation, Confirmation.

front: Qualities of a good user story
back: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

front: What a reviewer logs during individual review, before anyone has decided whether it really is a defect
back: Anomaly. Communication and analysis decides its status: defect, non-issue, question…

front: The review activity in which each reviewer works alone, e.g. with a checklist, and logs what looks wrong
back: Individual review.

front: The review activity in which logged anomalies are discussed and each gets a status, an owner and an action
back: Communication and analysis (usually the review meeting).

front: The review role that decides what is reviewed and provides the people and time
back: Manager. (Not the review leader: the leader organises who, when and where.)

front: The review role with overall responsibility: chooses who takes part and organises when and where
back: Review leader.

front: The review role that keeps meetings effective: mediation, time management, a safe place to speak
back: Moderator, also called facilitator.

front: The review role that collates the anomalies and records decisions and new anomalies from the meeting
back: Scribe, also called recorder.

front: The review type with no defined process and no formal documented output
back: Informal review. Main objective: detecting anomalies.

front: The review type led by the author, used to educate reviewers, gain consensus and generate ideas
back: Walkthrough. Individual preparation is optional.

front: The review type held by technically qualified reviewers and led by a moderator, to reach decisions on a technical problem
back: Technical review.

front: The review type that follows the complete process, aims at the maximum number of anomalies and collects metrics
back: Inspection: the most formal type. The author may not be review leader or scribe.

front: The one thing that must never be an objective of a review
back: Evaluating the participants.

front: Static testing finds ___ directly; dynamic testing causes ___ that must then be analysed
back: Defects; failures.

front: Tool category for testing that is hard or impossible by hand, such as generating load
back: Non-functional testing tools.

front: Tool category for the delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated builds and CI/CD
back: DevOps tools.

front: Tool category for virtual machines and containers
back: Tools supporting scalability and deployment standardisation.

front: Exact wording of the automation benefit about mistakes
back: Prevention of simple human errors through greater consistency and repeatability. Never "eliminates human error".

front: A commercial supplier may sell or retire the tool; a community project may stop. Which two automation risks?
back: Dependency on the tool vendor; open-source software that may be abandoned.

front: The automation risk about trusting the tool too much
back: Relying on the tool too much, e.g. ignoring the need for human critical thinking.

front: The five activities of the review process, in order
back: PIICF: Planning, review Initiation, Individual review, Communication and analysis, Fixing and reporting.

front: The success factors for reviews (nine)
back: Clear objectives and measurable exit criteria · the right review type · small chunks · feedback to authors and stakeholders · time to prepare · management support · part of the culture · training · facilitated meetings.

front: The test tool categories (eight, plus "any other")
back: Management · Static testing · Test design and implementation · Test execution and coverage · Non-functional testing · DevOps · Collaboration · Scalability and deployment standardisation. "My Static Team Executes Nightly; DevOps Chats Scale."

front: The six benefits of test automation
back: Time saved (repetitive work) · prevention of simple human errors (consistency, repeatability) · more objective assessment · easier access to information about testing · reduced execution times (earlier detection, faster feedback, faster time to market) · more time to design new, deeper tests.

front: The eight risks of test automation
back: Unrealistic expectations · inaccurate estimations of time, cost and effort · tool used where manual is better · over-reliance (no critical thinking) · vendor dependency · abandoned open source · not compatible with the platform · not compliant with regulations or safety standards.

front: The benefits of early and frequent stakeholder feedback
back: Quality problems communicated early · misunderstood or changed requirements caught earlier · the team understands what it builds · focus on the most valuable, risk-reducing features. Without it: rework, missed deadlines, blame, failure.

front: Technique family that derives tests from the specified behaviour, without looking at the internal structure
back: Black-box (specification-based) test techniques. Their tests survive a rewrite that keeps the behaviour.

front: Technique family whose tests depend on the design or code, so they can only be created once it exists
back: White-box (structure-based) test techniques.

front: Technique family whose effectiveness depends heavily on the tester's skills, and which finds defects the other families miss
back: Experience-based test techniques: error guessing, exploratory testing, checklist-based testing.

front: A partition of values the test object should process, or whose processing the spec defines
back: Valid partition. (Even a restricted or "nothing happens" outcome counts, if the spec defines it.)

front: A partition of values the test object should ignore or reject, or whose processing the spec does not define
back: Invalid partition. An error message in the spec does not make it valid.

front: Criterion for several inputs: every partition of every input used at least once, combinations ignored
back: Each Choice coverage. Minimum tests = the size of the largest set of partitions.

front: How equivalence partitioning coverage is calculated
back: Partitions exercised by at least one test ÷ partitions identified (valid and invalid) × 100%.

front: The minimum and maximum values of an ordered partition
back: Its boundary values. BVA needs ordered partitions.

front: For each boundary value: the value itself and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition
back: 2-value boundary value analysis. Range 1–60: 0, 1, 60, 61.

front: For each boundary value: the value itself and both its neighbours
back: 3-value boundary value analysis (more rigorous). Boundary values 1 and 60: 0, 1, 2, 59, 60, 61.

front: The coverage items of decision table testing
back: The columns with feasible combinations of conditions (not the N/A ones).

front: Decision table notation: "–" vs "N/A"
back: "–": the condition does not affect the outcome (the column still needs a test). "N/A": infeasible combination (no test).

front: Decision table where all conditions and actions are Boolean, vs one where some take several values
back: Limited-entry vs extended-entry decision table.

front: Number of columns in a full limited-entry decision table with n conditions
back: 2 to the power n (3 → 8, 4 → 16). Extended-entry: multiply the numbers of values.

front: The syntax of a transition label in a state transition diagram
back: event [guard condition] / action. Guard and action may be left out.

front: What the empty cells of a state table represent
back: Invalid transitions. A state table shows them explicitly; a diagram does not.

front: State transition criterion whose coverage items are the single valid transitions; the most widely used
back: Valid transitions coverage, also called 0-switch coverage.

front: State transition criterion that needs every valid transition exercised and every invalid one attempted
back: All transitions coverage: the minimum for mission- and safety-critical software.

front: Why only one invalid transition is tested per test case
back: To avoid fault masking: one defect hiding another.

front: The three state transition coverage criteria, weakest to strongest
back: All states < valid transitions (0-switch) < all transitions. Each full level guarantees the ones before it.

front: The coverage items of statement testing, and what 100% does not guarantee
back: Executable statements. 100% still misses data-dependent defects and untaken decision outcomes.

front: A transfer of control between two nodes of the control flow graph
back: A branch: unconditional (straight-line code) or conditional (a decision outcome: if, switch/case, loop).

front: Which coverage guarantees the other: statement or branch?
back: 100% branch coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage. Never the reverse.

front: The main weakness of white-box testing
back: Defects of omission: a requirement that was never implemented leaves no code to cover.

front: The fundamental strength of white-box testing
back: It takes the whole implementation into account, so it finds defects even when the spec is vague, outdated or incomplete.

front: The six areas where errors, defects and failures typically sit (error guessing)
back: Input · output · logic · computation · interfaces · data.

front: The way of structuring exploratory testing with a time-box, a charter and a debriefing
back: Session-based testing (with test session sheets for steps and discoveries).

front: The document that holds the test objectives guiding an exploratory session
back: Test charter. Its objectives act as high-level test conditions.

front: The three kinds of items that should NOT be on a test checklist
back: Items checkable automatically · items better as entry/exit criteria · items too general.

front: The effect of a high-level checklist on testing
back: More variability: potentially greater coverage, less repeatability.

front: The three perspectives that collaborative user-story writing brings together
back: Business, development and testing.

front: The two most common formats of acceptance criteria
back: Scenario-oriented (e.g. Given/When/Then, used in BDD) and rule-oriented (bullet-point list, input–output table).

front: What acceptance criteria are used for (five)
back: Scope of the story · consensus among stakeholders · positive and negative scenarios · basis for acceptance testing · accurate planning and estimation.

front: The first ATDD step, where the team analyses, discusses and writes the story and its acceptance criteria
back: Specification workshop.

front: The order in which ATDD test cases are written
back: Positive first, then negative, then non-functional (e.g. performance, usability).

front: What ATDD tests become when developers automate them in the team's framework while building the story
back: Executable requirements.

front: The document that sets out the objectives, resources and processes of a test project: the means and the schedule for reaching the test objectives
back: Test plan. Also a communication tool, and it shows how testing follows the test policy and test strategy.

front: Typical content of a test plan (seven parts)
back: Context of testing · assumptions and constraints · stakeholders · communication · risk register · test approach · budget and schedule.

front: The planning that looks ahead to the product's release and defines and re-defines the product backlog
back: Release planning. Testers: testable stories and acceptance criteria, risk analyses, test effort estimates, test approach, release test planning.

front: The planning that looks ahead to the end of one iteration and works on the iteration backlog
back: Iteration planning. Testers: detailed risk analysis of stories, testability, breaking stories into (testing) tasks, estimating them, refining functional and non-functional aspects.

front: The preconditions for starting an activity (resources, testware, initial quality of the test object)
back: Entry criteria. In Agile, for a user story: the Definition of Ready.

front: What must be achieved to declare an activity complete (thoroughness measures, yes/no criteria)
back: Exit criteria. In Agile: the Definition of Done. Running out of time or budget can also be one, if stakeholders accept the risk.

front: Metrics-based estimation that applies figures from the organisation's previous projects, such as a development-to-test effort ratio
back: Estimation based on ratios.

front: Metrics-based estimation that extends measurements taken as early as possible in the current project
back: Extrapolation.

front: Expert-based estimation: experts estimate alone, outliers explain, and the rounds repeat until consensus
back: Wideband Delphi. Planning Poker is its Agile variant.

front: The expert-based estimation formula using an optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) value
back: Three-point estimation: E = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6, standard deviation SD = (b − a) ÷ 6.

front: Prioritisation where the first test has the highest coverage and each next test adds the most coverage not yet reached
back: Additional coverage-based prioritisation.

front: The three test case prioritisation strategies, and the two things that can change the order
back: Risk-based · coverage-based · requirements-based. Order changed by dependencies (run them first) and resource availability.

front: The model of test granularity in which higher layers have fewer, slower, less isolated and more costly tests
back: Test pyramid. Original layers: unit, service, UI.

front: The four testing quadrants and what goes in each
back: Q1 tech/support: component, component integration (automated, CI) · Q2 business/support: functional, examples, story tests, UX prototypes, API, simulations · Q3 business/critique: exploratory, usability, UAT · Q4 tech/critique: smoke, non-functional except usability.

front: The measure of a risk, expressed by its likelihood and its impact
back: Risk level. The higher it is, the more important its treatment.

front: A risk about managing and controlling the project: organisational, people, technical or supplier issues
back: Project risk. If it happens: schedule, budget or scope suffer.

front: A risk about the quality characteristics of the product, such as wrong functions, poor response time or security holes
back: Product risk. If it happens: unhappy users, lost revenue or reputation, costs, penalties, even harm.

front: The two-part activity of risk identification and risk assessment
back: Product risk analysis. Goal: focus test effort to minimise residual product risk.

front: The two-part activity of risk mitigation and risk monitoring
back: Product risk control.

front: The four response options to an analysed product risk
back: Risk mitigation by testing · risk acceptance · risk transfer · contingency plan.

front: A corrective action taken in test control, such as reprioritising tests or adjusting the schedule
back: Control directive.

front: The seven groups of common test metrics
back: Project progress · test progress · product quality · defect · risk · coverage · cost.

front: The regular report that supports ongoing test control and lists the testing planned for the next period
back: Test progress report (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3: test status report).

front: The report written when a test level, type or project is finished, with deviations, unfixed defects and lessons learned
back: Test completion report.

front: An approved configuration item that can only be changed through formal change control
back: Baseline. You can revert to an earlier one to reproduce previous test results.

front: Typical content of a defect report from dynamic testing
back: ID · title · date, organisation, author and role · test object and environment · context · failure description with steps and evidence · expected and actual results · severity · priority · status · references.

front: The defect status after a fix has been delivered but not yet retested
back: Awaiting confirmation testing.

front: The ISTQB term for the flaw that a human mistake leaves in a work product (code, a requirement, a build file)
back: Defect (also called fault or bug). If the code containing it runs, it may cause a failure.

front: The ISTQB term for the system not doing what it should (or doing what it should not) while it runs
back: Failure. Caused by executing a defect, or by environmental conditions such as radiation or electromagnetic fields.

front: The activity of reproducing a failure, diagnosing its cause and fixing it
back: Debugging. Testing finds failures and defects; debugging removes the cause. Then: confirmation testing, regression testing.

front: The principle that a clean test run lowers the chance of hidden defects but can never prove there are none
back: Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects.

front: The principle behind using test techniques, prioritisation and risk instead of trying every input combination
back: Exhaustive testing is impossible.

front: The principle that removing defects in the requirements stops them spreading into the design and code
back: Early testing saves time and money.

front: The principle that a few components usually hold most of the defects (a Pareto pattern)
back: Defects cluster together. Used to focus risk-based testing.

front: The principle that the same tests, repeated unchanged, find fewer and fewer new defects
back: Tests wear out. Change tests and test data, or write new ones; automated regression is a useful exception.

front: The principle that there is no single approach to testing that fits every project
back: Testing is context dependent.

front: The principle that a well-verified, defect-free product can still fail because it does not meet users' needs
back: The absence-of-defects fallacy: validation is needed as well as verification.

front: Test analysis answers ___; test design answers ___
back: Analysis: WHAT to test (test conditions). Design: HOW to test (test cases, coverage items, data and environment requirements).

front: Testware produced by test planning
back: Test plan, test schedule, risk register, entry and exit criteria.

front: Testware produced by test monitoring and control
back: Test progress reports, documentation of control directives, risk information.

front: Testware produced by test analysis
back: Prioritised test conditions (e.g. acceptance criteria) and defect reports on defects in the test basis.

front: Testware produced by test design
back: Prioritised test cases, test charters, coverage items, test data requirements, test environment requirements.

front: Testware produced by test implementation
back: Test procedures, automated test scripts, test suites, test data, the test execution schedule, test environment elements (stubs, drivers, simulators, service virtualisation).

front: The two roles in testing, and the activities each mainly covers
back: Test management role: planning, monitoring and control, completion. Testing role: analysis, design, implementation, execution. One person may hold both at once.

front: The practice in which anyone with the right skills may do any task, the team shares a workspace and everyone is responsible for quality
back: The whole team approach (from Extreme Programming, XP).

front: The test-first approach in which tests direct the coding: write a test, write code to pass it, refactor
back: Test-driven development (TDD).

front: Test-first approaches: which one derives tests from acceptance criteria, and which one writes behaviour in natural language (Given/When/Then)?
back: ATDD: from acceptance criteria. BDD: desired behaviour in natural language, turned into executable tests.

front: The organisational approach that brings development (including testing) and operations together, with CI/CD and fast feedback
back: DevOps. Manual testing from the user's view is still needed.

front: The approach of moving testing earlier in the SDLC
back: Shift-left. Costs more early, expected to save more later; needs stakeholder buy-in.

front: The test level for interfaces between components, vs the one for interfaces with other systems and external services
back: Component integration testing vs system integration testing.

front: Acceptance testing at the developer's site vs at the users' own locations
back: Alpha testing vs beta testing.

front: Testing that the original defect is fixed vs testing that a change has broken nothing else
back: Confirmation testing vs regression testing. Impact analysis helps scope regression testing.

front: What retiring a system can require testing of
back: Data archiving (if data must be kept), and restore and retrieval procedures for the archived data.

front: Typical objectives of testing (nine)
back: Evaluate work products · trigger failures and find defects · ensure coverage · reduce the risk of poor quality · verify requirements are met · verify compliance (contract, law, regulation) · inform stakeholders' decisions · build confidence · validate it works as stakeholders expect.

front: Contextual factors that shape the test process (eight)
back: Stakeholders · team members · business domain · technical factors · project constraints · organisational factors · SDLC · tools.

front: Generic skills a tester needs, and what each gives
back: Testing knowledge (effectiveness) · thoroughness, curiosity, attention to detail (find hard defects) · communication, active listening, team player · analytical and critical thinking, creativity · technical knowledge (efficiency, tools) · domain knowledge (talk to users).

front: The four degrees of test independence, lowest to highest
back: None (the author) · some (peers in the same team) · high (another team in the organisation) · very high (outside the organisation). Usually use several.

front: Drawbacks of test independence
back: Isolation from developers (poor collaboration, communication problems, adversarial relationship) · developers lose responsibility for quality · testers seen as a bottleneck or blamed for delays.

front: What the chosen SDLC affects in testing (five)
back: Scope and timing of test activities (levels, types) · detail of test documentation · test techniques and approach · extent of automation · the tester's role and responsibilities.

front: Good testing practices for any SDLC (four)
back: A test activity for every development activity · different objectives per test level · test analysis and design start in the matching development phase · testers review drafts as soon as they exist.

front: DevOps for testing: benefits and risks
back: Benefits: fast feedback · CI supports shift-left · stable test environments · more focus on non-functional quality · less repetitive manual testing · lower regression risk. Risks: pipeline to define · CI/CD tools to maintain · automation needs resources.

front: Good practices for shift-left (five)
back: Review specs from a test view · write tests before code, run code in a test harness · CI/CD with automated component tests · static analysis before dynamic testing · non-functional testing from component level.

front: Benefits of retrospectives for testing (five)
back: Test effectiveness and efficiency · testware quality · team bonding and learning · test basis quality · cooperation between development and testing.

front: The five test levels
back: Component · component integration · system · system integration · acceptance.

front: The main forms of acceptance testing
back: User (UAT) · operational · contractual and regulatory · alpha (developer's site) · beta (users' sites). Ideally done by the intended users.

front: The four test types
back: Functional (WHAT it does) · non-functional (HOW WELL) · black-box (from the specification) · white-box (from the structure). All four at every level.

front: The triggers for maintenance testing (three)
back: Modifications (planned enhancements, corrective changes, hotfixes) · upgrades or migrations of the operational environment · retirement.
